strengths: Addresses important and practical problem of interpretability in retrosynthesis prediction with well-motivated approach combining LLMs and specialized models

Comprehensive experimental validation including multiple datasets (USPTO-50K/FULL, ChemBench, PaRoutes), diverse baselines, and especially compelling wet lab synthesis verification (79.3% and 58.82% yields) demonstrating real-world utility
Well-designed collaborative framework with clear three-stage pipeline and intuitive decision space construction that effectively leverages complementary strengths of specialized models and LLMs
Strong ablation studies (Tables 6-7) convincingly demonstrate necessity of decision space components and superiority of KGPO over SFT and GRPO, with clear mechanistic insights
Excellent out-of-distribution evaluation on ChemBench (94.66% of reactions absent from training) showing good generalization, and extension to multi-step retrosynthesis
Plug-and-play modularity allowing integration of different specialized models during inference without retraining, enhancing practical applicability
Comprehensive supplementary material with detailed reasoning examples (Figures 11-19) showing both successful selections and generations, and failure case analysis
weaknesses: Reward function design lacks principled justification: weight coefficients (α₁=1.5, α₂=1.0, α₃=0.2) appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis, and binary stage rewards (0/1) are coarse-grained, unable to capture partial correctness

Training uses only 9k samples from 40k available despite stratified sampling justification, with no analysis of information loss or sensitivity to training set size, limiting confidence in data efficiency claims
Self-correction capability (40.6% generation success) overstated—only applies to 68.7% of samples with all incorrect candidates, contributing modest ~3% improvement overall (Table 10)

Decision space complexity unaddressed: Cartesian product of 3 subtasks with 4 candidates each yields 64 paths, but computational complexity, search strategy, and scalability to larger spaces not discussed

Heavy dependence on specialized models without systematic analysis: if correct answer missing from Top-4 candidates, recovery rate limited to 40.6%; no evaluation of degradation with weaker component models
Empirical improvements modest relative to added complexity: 70.28% vs 67.2% (Graph2Edits) = 3.1% absolute gain; lacks statistical significance testing and confidence intervals

Incomplete interpretability evaluation: comparison only against single Qwen2.5-7B baseline; no comparison with human-written explanations, other interpretable ML approaches, or chain-of-thought prompting; inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) not reported
Limited wet lab validation: only 2 synthesis routes experimentally verified (selective examples); both involve relatively straightforward chemistry, limiting scope of validation
Potential fairness concern in comparisons: comparing 'LLM without space' vs 'LLM with space' conflates pure LLM capability with specialized model information, making advantage attribution unclear

Insufficient failure analysis: Figure 20 identifies two failure modes (multiple reactive sites, multiple pathways) but provides no proposed solutions; reliance on future 'domain-specific chemical heuristics' too vague
Arbitrary design choices: position shuffling ratios (5:3:2 to prevent reward hacking), temperature=0.7, max_completion_length=8192 lack ablation studies or justification
Missing critical analyses: no discussion of computational costs (training time, inference latency, memory), systematic biases by reaction type, or transferability to other chemical reasoning tasks

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: interpretability in retrosynthesis prediction, which is valuable for the chemistry domain
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL, ChemBench, PaRoutes) with diverse metrics and human expert assessment
Demonstrates practical utility through wet-lab validation of two novel synthesis routes with high yields (79.3% and 58.82%)
Shows strong generalization to out-of-distribution data (57% on ChemBench vs ~30% for general LLMs)
Exhibits model-agnostic compatibility with different specialized models without retraining (Table 2)
Well-motivated three-component architecture with clear roles for specialized models (precision), LLM (reasoning), and RL (optimization)
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily incremental: decision space construction is straightforward application of existing models; KGPO is weighted combination of standard reward signals; individual components (LLM reasoning, specialized subtasks, RL) are well-established
Overclaimed contributions: 'first retrosynthesis model capable of generating natural language interpretable reasoning' misleads given prior reasoning-based work (ChemCrow, Schwaller et al.)

Unfair experimental setup: general LLMs achieve 0.30% accuracy without decision space (Table 9) but 32.85% with it; the contribution of decision space vs. LLM reasoning strategy is conflated, making it unclear if the 70.28% improvement over Graph2Edits (67.2%, only ~3% gain) reflects novel reasoning or just privileged input

Weak technical justification: reward coefficients (α₁=1.5, α₂=1.0, α₃=0.2) lack principled justification; stage rewards (rᵢ) described as 'binary' but mechanically vague; no clarity on how correctness is extracted from LLM text or whether these are hand-crafted rules

Interpretability claims insufficiently supported: reasoning is evaluated indirectly against LLM assessment and human alignment with chemical principles (Table 5), not actual correctness; no rigorous validation that explanations explain predictions; examples appear cherry-picked

Serious reproducibility concerns: critical details missing (how stage rewards computed? Are they keyword-based rules? How sensitive is performance to specialized model choice?); no code availability; hyperparameter choices unexplained; KGPO implementation details sparse beyond objective function

Modest actual performance gains: 70.28% vs Graph2Edits 67.2% (~3%), and Table 2 shows LocalRetro and UAlign similarly improve with decision space, suggesting gains largely from the space itself rather than reasoning strategy; Table 3 shows only 2.2% improvement over EditRetro on larger dataset
Computational efficiency not addressed: approach requires running 3 specialized models per inference; latency/cost comparison to baselines missing; scalability implications unexplored

Limited failure analysis: fundamental limitations (multiple reactive sites, multiple transformation pathways) relegated to supplementary material (Figure 20) with insufficient discussion of when model should not be trusted

Weak ablation on core architectural choice: KGPO improves only 3.5% over GRPO (Table 7); unclear why this complexity is justified; Table 10 shows accuracy plateaus at 70.8% beyond 5 candidates, suggesting decision space saturation

strengths: Addresses an important and practically motivated problem: interpretability in retrosynthesis prediction, which is critical for real-world chemistry adoption
Well-designed collaborative framework synergizing specialized models (domain knowledge) with LLMs (reasoning capabilities) in a principled way
Novel KGPO reward mechanism encouraging 'right for the right reasons' reasoning through multi-stage rewards, effectively mitigating reward hacking
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL, ChemBench OOD) with systematic ablations validating core design choices
Strong out-of-distribution generalization (57% vs ~30-32% for general LLMs on ChemBench), demonstrating transferable reasoning learned through KGPO
Real wet-lab validation discovering novel synthesis routes with good experimental yields (79.3%, 58.82%), providing tangible evidence of practical utility
Model-agnostic compatibility enabling plug-and-play integration with different specialized models without retraining
Extensive supplementary materials with implementation details, diverse case studies, failure analysis, and human evaluation procedures supporting reproducibility
Rigorous ablation studies (Tables 6-7) demonstrating necessity of decision space components and effectiveness of KGPO over SFT/GRPO baselines
Clear problem formulation (Eq. 3) and technically sound approach building appropriately on established RL methods (GRPO)
weaknesses: Interpretability evaluation has significant gaps: only 3 human evaluators on undisclosed sample size, no inter-evaluator agreement metrics reported, and missing comparison against fair interpretability baselines or classical explainability methods

Framework exhibits strong dependence on specialized model quality; only 40.6% success rate when all candidates fail suggests limited robustness to weak specialized models without adequate analysis of failure modes

Design choices lack sufficient justification: reward weights (α₁=1.5, α₂=1.0, α₃=0.2) appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis, position shuffling ratio unjustified, and training data curation (9k from 50k) not ablated

Limited interpretability baseline comparisons: claims to be 'first' interpretable framework but doesn't compare against other interpretability-focused methods or classical explanation approaches; general LLM baselines are weak comparisons
Insufficient failure case analysis: only two failure modes identified without systematic characterization; fundamental limitations (site selectivity, multiple pathways) acknowledged but not addressed

Missing critical analyses: no inference time comparisons, no computational cost analysis despite long explanation generation, no prompt sensitivity ablation despite different prompts for different baselines
Weak multi-step retrosynthesis extension with only marginal improvement (38% vs 36%), and real-world applicability to chemistry workflows requiring selectivity and yield prediction remains unclear
Multi-stage reward design (Eq. 5) not compared against simpler final-answer-only rewards; improvements in reasoning quality metrics over GRPO (Table 7) are modest (~1 point on 5-point scales)
Training data stratification strategy claimed to improve generalization but not validated; no ablation comparing stratified vs. random sampling or sensitivity to training set size

Wet-lab validation limited to 2 examples and no comparison of prediction certainty, reaction conditions optimization, or practical workflow integration; missing user studies on whether explanations actually improve chemist decision-making

strengths: Addresses important problem of interpretability in retrosynthesis with well-motivated collaborative reasoning approach

Comprehensive evaluation including human expert assessment of reasoning quality, reasoning correctness validation (82.85% correct reasoning for correct answers), and wet lab validation of novel predicted routes
Strong empirical results: 75.69% Top-1 accuracy significantly outperforms baselines, with good OOD generalization (65.67% on ChemBench vs 32.54% for general LLMs)
Novel KGPO framework with chemistry-grounded reward model (Chem-RM) leveraging RDKit is principled and well-motivated
Demonstrates genuine coupling between reasoning quality and prediction correctness, with aligned intermediate and final decision correctness (Table 15)
Extensive supplementary material with detailed prompts, ablation studies, and reproducibility information
Extension to multi-step retrosynthesis with competitive results demonstrates extensibility of framework
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on pre-trained specialized models (T5Chem, GraphRetro) makes it difficult to isolate KGPO's contribution; Table 1 shows decision space causes larger performance swings than optimization algorithm, and Table 2 shows gains proportional to baseline model quality

7B LLM backbone size is a significant limitation; authors acknowledge chemical mistakes in verbalized rationales despite correct predictions, undermining interpretability claims and suggesting results would substantially improve with larger models

Experimental setup raises fairness concerns: Table 1's 'Space Setting' comparisons provide baselines with knowledge they weren't designed for; specialized models trained for direct prediction see 43-67% accuracy but 12-27% with Top-4 candidates—suggests comparison may not isolate method contribution

Reward model design insufficiently justified: hyperparameter choices (λ₁=1.5, λ₂=2.0, λ₃=1.0) lack ablation studies or sensitivity analysis; position shuffling to prevent reward hacking suggests potential reward misalignment

Training uses only 9k/80k samples rather than full datasets; unclear if improvements stem from data selection strategy or method; stratified sampling by template frequency could introduce sampling bias
Limited practical validation: only 2 wet lab cases out of ~5000 test samples; insufficient to support broad practical applicability claims; no analysis of synthesis difficulty or yield reliability

Failure modes inadequately addressed: Section F.3 identifies two failure classes (multiple reactive sites, multiple pathways) as persistent limitations with no clear solution beyond 'larger models'; these are common real-world challenges
Insufficient statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear if results from single runs or multiple seeds; incremental GRPO gains in Table 8 lack validation
Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for λ weights in reward function, no ablation for Top-K candidates in decision space, no evaluation of Top-3/Top-5 predictions for wet lab cases

Mixed decision consistency results suggest potential shortcuts: Table 15 shows 8.79% correct predictions despite wrong reaction type and 2.84% despite wrong reaction center; these cases need deeper analysis to confirm chemical soundness

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL, ChemBench) with human evaluation by chemistry PhDs
Addresses practically important problem of interpretable retrosynthesis with chemical grounding
Technical soundness of individual components (Chem-RM using RDKit, reasonable KGPO modifications)
Honest discussion of limitations in appendix; good presentation and documentation for reproducibility
Wet-lab validation demonstrating that at least two predicted syntheses are feasible
weaknesses: Misleading comparison setup: decision space alone provides ~29% improvement (Table 17) while KGPO only adds ~8.9%, conflating input advantage with algorithmic contribution

Interpretability claims are overstated: only 82.85% of correct predictions have correct reasoning (Table 5); reasoning quality scores are moderate (4.0-4.4/5.0); no evaluation of explanation faithfulness vs. post-hoc rationalization

Limited conceptual novelty: decision space is straightforward Cartesian product of Top-K candidates; KGPO is incremental modification to GRPO without strong theoretical justification; main contribution is engineering combination of existing techniques

Unfair baseline comparisons: models like ChemLLM not designed to accept reaction type/center inputs, making performance gains partially attributable to better input specification rather than algorithmic innovation

Minimal practical validation: only 2 wet-lab examples using well-established reactions (Suzuki coupling, Jones oxidation); insufficient to demonstrate genuine discovery capability; no documentation of example selection process or failure cases

Multi-step retrosynthesis extension is preliminary: simply reranks complete routes from specialized models rather than performing novel route planning; authors acknowledge need for more systematic development
Design choices lack justification: reward weights (λ₁=1.5, λ₂=2.0, λ₃=1.0) have no ablation; position shuffling ratio (5:3:2) unexplained; Top-4 candidates suboptimal per Table 18 (stabilizes at N≥5)
Training uses curated 9K/80K subset of full datasets (50K/1M) due to distribution skewing; unclear how much curation contributes to reported performance; generalization concerns

strengths: Well-motivated framework addressing genuine limitations of existing retrosynthesis methods: lack of interpretability, limited logical reasoning, and weak grounding in chemical principles
Strong empirical results with 75.69% Top-1 accuracy on USPTO-50K, 16.77% improvement over same-backbone SFT baseline, and excellent out-of-distribution generalization (65.67% on ChemBench)

Genuine interpretability advances validated by human evaluation: 82.85% of correct predictions have correct reasoning vs. 33.60% for incorrect ones; reasoning causally coupled with predictions (64.06% consistency)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets with human evaluation by 3 chemistry PhDs, high inter-annotator agreement (83% unanimous), and decision consistency analysis
Wet-lab validation discovering two novel synthesis routes with confirmed yields (79.3% and 58.82%), demonstrating practical utility beyond in-silico metrics

Technical contributions: Chemical Decision Space construction (ablation: 29.1% → 75.7% with type+center+reactants), Chem-RM using deterministic chemical tools, KGPO with principled advantage rectification

Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of components; behavior analysis showing 95.71% candidate-grounded reasoning; self-correction mechanism achieves 43.1% success when all candidates incorrect
Clear problem motivation, well-structured presentation with extensive appendices; code availability promised for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: chemical decision space is straightforward application of existing specialized models; KGPO is incremental modification of GRPO (similar to DeepSeekMath); main contribution is architectural integration rather than algorithmic innovation

Strong dependence on specialized models with performance ceiling bounded by their accuracy; framework requires high-quality T5Chem and GraphRetro; robustness to lower-quality specialized models unexplored; training uses curated 9k subset raising generalization questions

Model scale limitation: uses only 7B backbone (small by 2025 standards); authors explicitly acknowledge this limits 'local structural analysis ability,' causing potential errors in verbalized rationales despite correct decisions; scalability to larger models unexplored

Incomplete multi-step retrosynthesis: only 2 wet-lab examples for multi-step validation, limited baseline comparisons, authors acknowledge 'more systematic development needed' (Appendix I); route-level reasoning simpler than step-level

Reward model design concerns: r_struct uses set-based functional group matching missing structural nuances; r_react relies on indicator functions without partial credit; entirely rule-based without learned components; sensitivity to λ weights not explored

Evaluation limitations: OOD dataset small (300 examples) without confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; no multiple random seeds reported; evaluation only on USPTO data; generalization to other domains/reaction types unknown

Reasoning quality caveats: 17.15% of correct predictions have only partially correct reasoning; 66.4% of incorrect predictions have mixed/incorrect reasoning; Table 14 shows 19% both wrong answer and wrong reasoning; reasoning doesn't guarantee correctness

Missing critical analysis: no computational cost comparison; limited error analysis (only 2 failure cases); no human chemist study validating utility of explanations; incomplete sensitivity analyses; failure modes not systematically categorized

Statistical rigor issues: no confidence intervals, error bars, or p-values; small OOD dataset especially needs testing; ablation studies lack error estimates; claims about causal coupling of reasoning and predictions based on aggregate statistics rather than individual-level analysis

Scope limitations: all experiments on USPTO atom-mapped reactions; circular evaluation (specialized models trained on same data); generalization to novel reaction types, rare scaffolds, or different chemical domains unexplored
